agent_summary:
Worked the Business Logic lane against juice.lab.test (OWASP Juice Shop v20.2.0) with 60 read-only requests; no writes (disallowed) and no test accounts were available.

Done:
- BUSL-01 (data validation): /rest/products/search?q=') returns a 500 SQLITE_ERROR (unsanitised concatenation), while /rest/deluxe-membership and the security-question email param apply server-side validation — validation is inconsistent.
- BUSL-02 (forging requests): /rest/track-order/{id} returns order data with no session (forgeable), object APIs (basket, Cards, Addresss, BasketItems, SecurityAnswers) correctly 401; wildcard CORS (ACAO:*) on all responses eases cross-origin reads.
- BUSL-03 (integrity): /rest/captcha returns its own answer; /api/Quantitys exposes limitPerUser caps and /api/Deliverys exposes prices (incl. a 0-cost option) unauth; products expose price/deluxePrice — all client-influenced values the server must revalidate at checkout.
- BUSL-05 (function-use limits): CAPTCHA answer disclosure defeats feedback anti-automation; no rate limiting seen across ~60 requests; /rest/image-captcha does require login.
- BUSL-06 (workflow circumvention): track-order bypass vs. server-guarded steps (deluxe eligibility, order-history/dataerasure "Blocked illegal activity").
- BUSL-07 (misuse defenses): weak/inconsistent — unauthenticated browsable /support/logs leaks access logs containing session tokens/emails (10 redacted by gateway), unauth browsable /encryptionkeys, verbose Express stack traces, user enumeration via security-question; some abuse detection exists ("Blocked illegal activity").
- BUSL-08 (unexpected file types): /ftp fileserver enforces a .md/.pdf allowlist (403), upload endpoints accept POST, uploads land in the browsable /ftp/quarantine; a documented null-byte allowlist bypass already exists.

N/A:
- BUSL-04 (process timing) and BUSL-09 (malicious file upload): both require authenticated/POST actions that cannot be performed read-only and no test accounts were provided.

Leads recorded: CAPTCHA answer disclosure, /support/logs token/email leak (medium), security-question user enumeration, /api/Quantitys limitPerUser exposure + Quantitys list vs item authz inconsistency, /encryptionkeys and /ftp/quarantine browsable directories. Reachable paths confirmed include /, /rest/admin/application-configuration, /rest/captcha, /api/Feedbacks, /rest/products/search, /rest/products/{id}/reviews, /api/Quantitys, /api/Deliverys, /api/SecurityQuestions, /rest/track-order/{id}, /rest/user/security-question, /metrics, /ftp (+quarantine), /support/logs, /encryptionkeys. A reviewer should validate the logs/token exposure and the Quantitys write path.

leads.title: [agent] Broken access control & browsable upload quarantine: /api/Quantitys list readable unauth while /api/Quantitys/{id} is 403; /ftp/quarantine listable

detail.text: GET /api/Quantitys returns the full quantity/limitPerUser table with no auth (200), yet GET /api/Quantitys/1 returns 403 — inconsistent authorization on the same resource (list endpoint under-protected). Separately, GET /ftp/quarantine (the folder where uploaded complaint attachments are stored) returns a browsable 200 directory listing with no auth, so any file accepted by the upload validator becomes anonymously downloadable.

leads.title: [agent] CAPTCHA answer disclosed in /rest/captcha response (defeats feedback anti-automation limit)

detail.text: GET /rest/captcha returns JSON {"captchaId":0,"captcha":"9*8+10","answer":"82"} — the expected answer is sent to the client alongside the challenge. A client can read the answer and submit it, defeating the CAPTCHA's purpose of limiting how often the feedback/complaint function can be used. Unauthenticated, read-only reproduction.

leads.title: [agent] Per-user purchase limits (limitPerUser) exposed unauthenticated via /api/Quantitys

detail.text: GET /api/Quantitys (no auth) returns the full product quantity table including stock levels and limitPerUser values (e.g. ProductId 1 limitPerUser 5). This discloses the business-rule purchase caps to anonymous clients; in Juice Shop this table is also writable by non-admins, but that would require a write to confirm.

GET /encryptionkeys returns HTTP 200 with a ~8KB serve-index HTML directory listing and no authentication. In OWASP Juice Shop this folder holds cryptographic key material; exposing a browsable listing of it to anonymous callers is an access-control/information-disclosure weakness. (Body not re-read here to conserve budget; status 200 + text/html directory confirmed.)

leads.title: [agent] Unauthenticated browsable /support/logs exposes access logs containing auth tokens and emails

detail.text: GET /support/logs returns a serve-index directory listing (access.log.2026-10-16, audit.json) with no authentication. GET /support/logs/access.log.2026-10-16 (200, 15KB) returns the raw HTTP access log; the gateway reported replacing 10 sensitive values (token, email address) that appeared in logged request URLs/strings, confirming the log leaks session tokens and user emails to any anonymous caller. audit.json also discloses internal paths (/juice-shop/logs/...) and file hashes. This is a logging/monitoring access-control failure (application misuse defense).

GET /rest/user/security-question?email=admin@juice-sh.op (no auth) returns {"question":{"id":2,"question":"Mother's maiden name?"...}} for an existing account, disclosing the account's configured security question. A non-existent email returns an empty object, so the endpoint lets an anonymous caller enumerate which emails are registered and which security question each uses — useful for targeting the forgot-password flow.

[agent] GET http://juice.lab.test/ftp/package.json.bak -> 403. Examined file-type handling reachable read-only: the /ftp fileserver enforces a ".md and .pdf only" allowlist (403 on package.json.bak), the complaint upload endpoints (OPTIONS /file-upload, /profile/image/file) accept POST, uploaded files land in the browsable /ftp/quarantine folder, and /metrics exposes file_uploads_count/file_upload_errors counters. Actually submitting an unexpected file type requires a POST (writes disallowed this lane), so the upload itself was not exercised; a documented null-byte allowlist-bypass lead already exists for the fileserver side.
